content: An infusion set is a critical component of intensive insulin therapy, used in conjunction with an insulin pump to deliver insulin subcutaneously. It consists of a complete tubing system that connects the insulin pump to the user. The infusion set includes several key components: a subcutaneous cannula, an adhesive mount, a quick-disconnect mechanism, and a connector for the pump cartridge. To use an infusion set, the user must first attach a reservoir of insulin to the set and connect it to the pump. The system is then primed, a process in which the pump rapidly pushes insulin through the tubing and cannula to eliminate any air bubbles. It is essential that the infusion set is not inserted into the skin during priming, as this could result in the accidental delivery of a large and potentially dangerous dose of insulin. Once priming is complete, the user removes the protective paper from the adhesive pad and carefully inserts the needle beneath the skin. The cannula, typically made of flexible plastic, is designed to remain in place comfortably under the skin. During insertion, the needle carries the cannula into the subcutaneous fat layer and is then withdrawn, leaving the cannula in place. The insertion should be performed in a swift motion to prevent the cannula from bunching around the needle. Some users may prefer infusion sets with a steel needle instead of a plastic cannula. In these cases, the steel needle, similar to a hypodermic syringe, remains in place under the skin. For those who find manual insertion challenging or uncomfortable, spring-loaded insertion devices are available. These devices are designed to insert the needle quickly and with minimal discomfort. The user loads the primed infusion set into the device, removes the protective paper from the adhesive pad, positions the device against the skin, and presses a button to complete the insertion. This method is particularly beneficial for individuals with needle phobia. The most common site for infusion set placement is the abdomen, typically in a semicircular area around and below the navel. Other viable sites include the upper thighs, upper buttocks, hips, upper arms, and lower back. Insulin absorption rates can vary depending on the site, so patients should consult their diabetes care team to determine the most effective locations for their infusion sets. To maintain optimal insulin absorption and blood glucose control, infusion sets must be replaced every 2-3 days. Prolonged use of the same site can lead to reduced insulin absorption and suboptimal glucose management. When changing the infusion set, the site should also be rotated to prevent tissue damage or lipohypertrophy. Infusion sets can be disconnected from the pump and tubing using a quick-release mechanism, which leaves the cannula and adhesive pad in place. This feature is particularly useful during activities such as swimming or showering, as most insulin pumps are not fully waterproof, or during other situations where being attached to the pump is inconvenient. There are various types of infusion sets available, offering users the ability to customize their setup based on individual needs. These sets differ in cannula length, the angle of cannula insertion, and the length of the tubing connecting the cannula to the pump. For example, individuals with minimal body fat may prefer a shorter cannula that enters the skin at a shallow angle, while those with more body fat may benefit from a longer cannula inserted at a right angle. Most infusion sets use a standard Luer Lock connector, which is compatible with most insulin pumps. However, some pump manufacturers use proprietary connectors, requiring users to purchase infusion sets specific to their pump model. For assistance in selecting the most appropriate infusion set, users are encouraged to consult their certified diabetes educator or reach out to support groups for insulin pump users. Additional information can also be found on the websites of infusion set manufacturers.
